title: Two Right Angles, the Rest 160°: How Many Sides? | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: A partial convex shape (same as the question scene): two right-angle corners at the bottom-right, a few 160° corners, and the rest of the outline dashed/unknown, so the side count is NOT shown. Line 2: a walking arrow traces the known part of the boundary. Line 3: Vantee title card. Keep the real 11-gon for the 'count' scene.
lines: A shape with two square corners, and every other corner is one hundred sixty degrees. How many sides?
Adding up the inside angles works, but there's a neater trick: take a walk around the outside.
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's go for a walk.

scenes.visual: Question text left; on the right a generic convex shape outline with two right-angle marks and a few corners labeled 160° (the rest shown as '…' — not the exact 11-gon, so the side count isn't given away; e.g. a partial shape with a dashed unknown part). Line 4: chips 9, 10, 11, 12, 20.
lines: Here's the question.
A convex polygon has exactly two interior angles of ninety degrees.
Every other interior angle is one hundred sixty degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

scenes.visual: Line 1: 'convex' card with a small example (all corners poke outward) vs a dented shape crossed out. Line 2: '2 corners: 90°', 'all others: 160°'. Line 3: 'sides = corners = ?'.
lines: So what do we know? Convex means every corner points outward. No dents.
Two corners are ninety degrees. All the others are one hundred sixty degrees.
A polygon has as many sides as corners. So let's count the corners.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; question visible.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Use a simple example first: a square, then a pentagon. Line 2: arrow walks along the square, turning at each corner (green outside turn arc); 'turns: 90 + 90 + 90 + 90 = 360'. Line 3: same walk on a lopsided pentagon, turn arcs collect into a full circle at the center ('360°'). Line 4: at one corner, interior (purple) + turn (green) on a straight line: 'inside + turn = 180'.
lines: Welcome back! Here's the strategy: walk around the outside of the shape, and add up your turns.
Walk around a square. You turn ninety degrees at each corner, four times. That's three hundred sixty.
Here's the amazing part.
You end up facing the way you started, so you've spun around once.
For any convex shape, your turns always add up to one full circle, three hundred sixty degrees.
At each corner, the inside angle and the turn sit on a straight line. Together they make one hundred eighty.

scenes.visual: Now the real 11-gon (from verify.py). Line 1: at a right-angle corner: '180 − 90 = 90' turn. Line 2: at a 160° corner: '180 − 160 = 20' turn. Line 3: the two 90° turns fill half of a turn-circle: '360 − 90 − 90 = 180'. Line 4: '180 ÷ 20 = 9' — 20° wedges fill the other half one by one, counter ×1…×9, while the walking arrow passes each 160° corner. Line 5: '9 + 2 = 11'. Line 6: answer badge '11 sides' with chime at line end, choice C highlighted.
lines: At a ninety degree corner, you turn one hundred eighty minus ninety, which is ninety degrees.
At a corner of one hundred sixty degrees, you turn just twenty degrees.
The two square corners use up ninety plus ninety, one hundred eighty degrees of turning.
That leaves one hundred eighty.
Each of the other corners turns twenty degrees. One hundred eighty divided by twenty is nine corners.
Nine corners plus the two square ones makes eleven corners, so eleven sides.
The polygon has eleven sides. That's Choice C!

scenes.visual: Line 1: card 'n sides → inside angles add to (n − 2) × 180'; a pentagon split into 3 triangles from one corner. Line 2: '2 × 90 + (n − 2) × 160'. Line 3: '(n − 2) × 180 = 180 + (n − 2) × 160'. Line 4: '(n − 2) × 20 = 180', 'n − 2 = 9', 'n = 11'. Line 5: card.
lines: Here's another way.
A shape with n sides splits into n minus two triangles.
So its inside angles add to n minus two, times one hundred eighty.
Our shape has two ninety degree corners, and n minus two corners of one hundred sixty.
So n minus two times one hundred eighty, equals one hundred eighty, plus n minus two times one hundred sixty.
n minus two groups of one hundred eighty, take away n minus two groups of one hundred sixty, leaves n minus two groups of twenty.
And that equals one hundred eighty.
So n minus two is nine, and n is eleven. Same answer!
When would you pick this way? When you like equations. The walk is quicker when lots of corners match.

scenes.visual: Choice chips; wrong ones turn red. Line 2: the 9 counter from solution 1 with '+ 2 forgotten'. Line 3: a 20° turn wedge labeled '20 = a turn, not a count'. Line 4: rows '10 sides: should be 1440, ours 1460' and '12 sides: should be 1800, ours 1780', both red.
lines: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
Choice A, nine, counts only the one hundred sixty degree corners. Don't forget the two square ones!
Choice E, twenty, is the turn at each of those corners, twenty degrees.
That's an angle, not a number of sides.
Choices B and D, ten and twelve, fail the angle check.
Ten sides should add to one thousand four hundred forty. But two corners of ninety and eight of one hundred sixty add to one thousand four hundred sixty.
Twelve sides should add to one thousand eight hundred. But two corners of ninety and ten of one hundred sixty add to one thousand seven hundred eighty.
So here's a great habit. For polygon angles, think about the turns. They always add up to three hundred sixty.

scenes.visual: Variant card: 'convex polygon: three angles of 120°, all others 150°'.
lines: Ready for a challenge? A convex polygon has exactly three angles of one hundred twenty degrees.
Every other angle is one hundred fifty degrees. How many sides does it have?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant card visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!
Let's walk it. At each one hundred twenty degree corner you turn sixty degrees.
Three of them make one hundred eighty.
That leaves one hundred eighty degrees of turning for the other corners.
Each one hundred fifty degree corner turns thirty degrees. One hundred eighty divided by thirty is six.
Six corners plus three makes nine sides!
Check: nine sides means inside angles of one thousand two hundred sixty.
Three times one hundred twenty, plus six times one hundred fifty, is one thousand two hundred sixty. It works!
If you got nine, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: walking arrow around a polygon, 'turns add to 360°', 'turn = 180 − inside angle'.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
Walk around a convex shape, and your turns always add up to three hundred sixty degrees.
Subtract the turns you know, then divide what's left by the turn at each other corner.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
